newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coup leaders under Nigerian pressure.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coup leaders under Nigerian pressure.

text.p: Sierra Leone rebel leader Foday Sankoh on Wednesday ordered his forces to back leaders of a weekend coup as regional power Nigeria kept up pressure for restoration of the civilian president.

Freetown's new military leader Major Johnny Paul Koromah tried to reassure Sierra Leoneans at his first news conference that Nigerian ships which landed hundreds of troops on Tuesday had come to evacuate their nationals, not to intervene.
But a senior military source said Koromah's Armed Forces Revolutionary Council was under strong pressure to stand aside.

A Middle East Airlines plane took off from Ghana for Freetown's Lungi airport to fly out 150 Lebanese nationals. United Nations officials and diplomats met Koromah to discuss an evacuation of a U.N.-chartered boat which arrived on Tuesday.
Koromah said there was no cause for alarm. "ECOMOG will not interfere in our internal matters," he said, referring to the Nigerian-led regional force in Liberia and Sierra Leone.

Nigeria has made no public statement on Sunday's coup but officials said it was trying to negotiate a peaceful restoration of civilian president Ahamd Tejan Kabbah. Senior Nigerian army officers were expected in Freetown later in the day.
A Nigerian military spokesman said the most likely person to lead the team was Major-General Abdulsalam Abubakar, the chief of defence staff and a confidant of military ruler General Sani Abacha.

Abubakar is the number three in the Nigerian military and is well known to the Sierra Leone army with whom he renewed a Status of Services Agreement in March under which Nigeria trains Sierra Leone's army and police.
Sankoh, in a broadcast on Sierra Leone radio, said his Revolutionary United Front (RUF) rebels and the army now had common cause and he wanted to come home and join the government.

"All RUF field commanders and troops should stand by for any reinforcement needed by Major Koromah to defend our sovereignty," said Sankoh, who is currently held at a hotel in the Nigerian capital. "The politicians are our enemies, not the army."
A peace accord signed by Sankoh and Kabbah has failed to hold, and Sankoh is reported to be disillusioned with its terms.

Koromah has banned political activity and suspended the civilian constitution. His council banned a demonstration called by civilian opponents of the coup for Wednesday to demand the return of Kabbah, whose civilian government was elected in March 1996 after four years of military rule.
At his news conference he apologised for the widespread looting. Asked about the fire at the central bank he described it as "a bad start for my government economically".
Shops, offices and schools were closed, but schoolchildren headed for examination centres hoping to sit examinations cancelled on Tuesday.
Shooting could be heard in Freetown overnight, and protests against the coup have been reported from towns in the interior.
Nigeria landed 720 troops at Freetown's port and airport on Tuesday to reinforce the 900 already stationed in the country.
Sierra Leone's U.N. ambassador James Jonah said Kabbah had appealed to West African countries "for help to restore democracy" which could include the use of troops.
The U.N. Security Council joined African and Western governments in condemning the coup and accompanying violence and called for "an immediate restoration of constitutional order".

The U.S. navy helicopter ship Kearsarge with 1,200 Marines headed for Sierra Leone from the waters off Zaire, where it had been on standby for a possible evacuation during the final days of Mobutu Sese Seko's rule.
"An American warship entering the waters of Sierra Leone is provocative," Sankoh told Reuter. "They should rest assured that their nationals are safe."
At least 40 people, including two Nigerian soldiers, were killed and twice that number wounded in fighting on Sunday, hospital sources said.
